sources.note: Nothing. Introduction (p. i) gives a vowel chart and 'Tones: There are three level tones and two glides, falling and rising'; no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the 76 pp. (a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent/prominence absent).

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2010. Iten consonant alternation and its possible historical origins. Circulation draft, Cambridge, 30 August 2010. 14 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on Iten stress. Sec. 3.2.2 'The sound system of Iten' (pp. 3-4) gives consonants, prosodies (labialisation/palatalisation) and 'Tones: There are three level tones and one glides, falling.' Sec. 2.2 contrasts Atlantic languages ('no tone, accent systems or restricted tone') with Central Nigerian languages having 'complex tonal systems'.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2006. Comparative Beromic. Ms., 25 pp. (comparative wordlist tables: Berom dialects, Iten, Cara, Shall-Zwall).
Bouquiaux, Luc. 1964. A word list of Aten (Ganawuri). Journal of West African Languages 1(2): 5-25.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Intro notes (pp. 5-7, French) describe a Berom-like tone system: three registers (haut, moyen, bas), six contour combinations, an extra-low tone probably non-phonemic, vowel length; author states the survey was too brief for phonological analysis and notation is purely phonetic. Image-only scan; pages read visually and scanned of pp. 5-7.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2018. Nominal affixes and number marking in the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. In John R. Watters (ed.), East Benue-Congo: Nouns, pronouns, and verbs (Niger-Congo Comparative Studies 1), 107-172. Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.1314325
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog benu1248). The only tone statement is family-level (p. 111: most Plateau languages have a three-level tone system, mid unmarked by convention); for Iten specifically the number-marking summary lists prefix alternation and consonant mutation but, unlike Cara ('tone and length contrasts'), no tonal marking; nothing on the Iten tone inventory itself.

tone.quote: Some of the earliest data is not tone-marked, and the segmental transcription may be less reliable. Most Plateau languages have a three-level tone system and by convention the mid-tone is not marked. Therefore, if the data is tone-marked, a vowel without a tone is deemed to be mid.
tone.locator: p. 111, sec. 1 (transcription conventions); Iten rows in Table 2 (p. 114) and Table 13 (p. 121)
tone.summary: Family-level statement only: Plateau languages generally 3 level tones (H, M, L; M unmarked); no Iten-specific tone inventory or tonal number-marking reported (Iten plural = prefix alternation + consonant mutation).
tone.says: The only tone statement is family-level (p. 111: most Plateau languages have a three-level tone system, mid unmarked by convention); for Iten specifically the number-marking summary lists prefix alternation and consonant mutation but, unlike Cara ('tone and length contrasts'), no tonal marking; nothing on the Iten tone inventory itself.
